t.4.30.1: Then Rāma's younger brother, the king's son of undaunted spirit, spoke thus to his elder brother, the son of the lord of men, who was full of longing, dejected, overcome with grief, and whose anger had flared up.
t.4.30.2: The monkey will not abide in good conduct, nor will he consider the consequences bound up with the fruit of his task; he will not long enjoy the royal fortune of the monkeys, for indeed his mind does not proceed in that direction.
t.4.30.3: Through the loss of his judgment he is attached to vulgar pleasures and has no thought of repaying your kindness; let him be slain and behold his elder brother Vālin. The kingdom should not be given in this way to one so devoid of virtue.
t.4.30.4: I cannot hold back my anger, whose force has surged up; today I will slay the faithless Sugrīva. Let the son of Vālin, together with the foremost of the monkeys, carry out the search for the wife of the lord of men.
t.4.30.5: To him, who had taken up his bow and was springing forth, fierce in his wrath in battle, the matter having been made known to him, Rāma, slayer of enemy heroes, spoke words well considered and full of gentle conciliation.
t.4.30.6: Surely no one like you in this world would commit such a sin. He who strikes down a wicked man by noble means is a hero, the best of men.
t.4.30.7: Today, Lakṣmaṇa, you who are of virtuous conduct must not take this course. Keep to that affection and to the friendship formed before.
t.4.30.9: Thus duly instructed in his purpose by his elder brother, that bull among men, the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes, entered the city.
t.4.30.8: With words imbued with conciliation and avoiding harsh ones, you should speak to Sugrīva, who has let the appointed time slip past.
t.4.30.10: Then Lakṣmaṇa, wise and pure of mind, devoted to the welfare and pleasure of his brother, went in great wrath to the dwelling of the monkey.
t.4.30.11: Like Kāla the Destroyer, he grasped his bow, which resembled the bow of Śakra and looked like a mountain peak, and he appeared like Mandara with its lofty ridges.
t.4.30.12: Then Rāma's younger brother, who always did as he was told and who equalled Bṛhaspati in intelligence, considered the message along with the reply and the rejoinder to it.
t.4.30.13: Enveloped by the fire of his brother's anger, which had arisen from longing and wrath, Lakṣmaṇa then set forth, displeased, like a raging storm-wind.
t.4.30.14: With great force he felled many sāla, tāla and aśvakarṇa trees, and in his swift rush he flung aside mountain peaks and other trees.
t.4.30.15: Shattering rocks to pieces with his feet, moving swiftly like an elephant, he left the narrow footpath far behind and went on quickly, driven by the urgency of his task.
t.4.30.16: The tiger of the Ikṣvākus beheld Kiṣkindhā, that great city of the king of the monkeys, crowded with troops, impregnable, lying within a mountain defile.
t.4.30.18: Within the mountains, the vānaras, resembling elephants, seized mountain peaks by the hundreds and full-grown trees.
t.4.30.17: Lakṣmaṇa, his lips quivering with rage against Sugrīva, saw the fearsome monkeys roaming outside Kiṣkindhā.
t.4.30.19: But Lakṣmaṇa, seeing those monkeys with weapons in hand, became twice as enraged, like a fire fed with much fuel.
t.4.30.20: Seeing him enraged, resembling Kāla, Death, and the end of the age, those monkeys, their limbs seized with fear, fled by the hundreds in all directions.
t.4.30.21: Then the foremost of the monkeys, having entered Sugrīva's palace, reported both the anger and the arrival of Lakṣmaṇa.
t.4.30.22: The bull among monkeys, lustful and absorbed in pleasure, remained in seclusion together with Tārā, and at that time he did not heed the words of those heroic monkeys.
t.4.30.23: Then, instructed by the ministers, the monkeys, hair-raising to behold and resembling mountains, elephants and clouds, went forth from the city.
t.4.30.24: Fearsome, with claws and fangs for weapons, all of them were of hideous appearance; all possessed the pride of tigers, and all had misshapen faces.
t.4.30.25: Some had the strength of ten elephants, some ten times more than that, and some were equal in valour to a thousand elephants.
t.4.30.26: The enraged Lakṣmaṇa beheld that unassailable Kiṣkindhā, wholly filled with mighty monkeys bearing trees in their hands.
t.4.30.27: Then all those monkeys of towering strength came forth from the space between the rampart and the moat and stood there in full view.
t.4.30.29: That tiger among men, heaving long, hot and mighty sighs, his eyes reddened with anger, became like a fire wreathed in smoke.
t.4.30.28: Realizing Sugrīva's negligence, and that his elder brother was distressed and in the grip of anger, the self-possessed hero set out once more.
t.4.30.30: With the barbed heads of his arrows for a flickering tongue, his bow for a serpent's coiled body, and his own fiery energy for a mass of venom, he was like a five-mouthed serpent.
t.4.30.31: Approaching him, who was like the blazing fire of universal destruction and like an enraged lord of serpents, Aṅgada, out of fear, fell into deep despair.
t.4.30.33: Here Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma's younger brother, the subduer of foes, has come into your presence; tormented by his brother's distress, he stands at the gate.
t.4.30.32: He of great fame, his eyes copper-red with anger, instructed Aṅgada: "Dear child, let Sugrīva be told of my arrival."
t.4.30.34: Hearing Lakṣmaṇa's words, Aṅgada, overcome with grief, went to his father's side and said, "Saumitri has come."
t.4.30.35: Seeing him, they all together raised near Lakṣmaṇa a lion's roar that was like a mighty flood, its sound like that of a thunderbolt.
t.4.30.38: Plakṣa and Prabhāva, the two ministers for matters of wealth and righteousness, announced that Lakṣmaṇa had arrived to speak words both harsh and mild.
t.4.30.37: Then, having heard Aṅgada's words, the two esteemed and noble-sighted counsellors of the lord of monkeys came together with him.
t.4.30.40: The brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, true to their word and greatly fortunate, worthy of kingship and bestowers of kingdoms, have entered into friendship with you.
t.4.30.39: Having appeased Sugrīva with words firmly grounded in conciliation, the two sat in attendance upon him as he sat, just as attendants wait upon Śakra, lord of the Maruts.
t.4.30.36: At that great sound the monkey awoke, his eyes copper-red and bewildered with intoxication, his garlands and ornaments in disarray.
t.4.30.41: One of those two, Lakṣmaṇa, stands at the gate with bow in hand; afraid of him, the monkeys tremble and let out cries.
t.4.30.42: Here has come Lakṣmaṇa, the brother of Rāghava, by the command of that Rāma, with his words as his charioteer and firm resolve as his chariot.
t.4.30.43: Bowing your head to him, together with your son and your kinsmen, O king, abide by your own agreement and be true to your promise.
